title: Simple Linear Regression and OLS
abstract:
The first supervised algorithm. Simple linear regression finds the best-fit line
through the data — the line with the lowest possible error from each point —
and Ordinary Least Squares solves for it exactly, in closed form. This document
derives both coefficients from scratch by differentiating the error function,
shows why the squared error is used rather than the absolute error, gives the
geometric and matrix views, states the assumptions that make the solution valid,
and explains precisely when OLS is preferable to gradient descent.

blocks.t: The Setup
From the notes
Linear regression is a supervised ML algorithm. Three types:

items: Simple Linear Regression — 1 input column, 1 output column.
Multiple Linear Regression — more than 1 input column, 1 output.
Polynomial Linear Regression — when the data is not linear.

blocks.t:
This topic covers the first. Multiple linear regression is Topic 36; polynomial
regression is Topic 39.
What simple linear regression does

items: with the lowest possible error from each point.

blocks.t: \boxed{ y = mx + c }
The goal is to find optimal $m$ and $c$.

blocks.cap:
Left: infinitely many lines pass through a cloud of points; we need a
 criterion. Middle: the criterion — the vertical distances $d_i$ from each
 point to the line. Right: the residual plot, the standard diagnostic that the
 line is appropriate.

blocks.t: Note on $c$ from the notes

$c$ is the offset — how far above or below the origin the line sits.
Two lines with the same slope but different intercepts are parallel; the one with
the larger $|c|$ has the higher offset. Fitting $c$ freely is what lets the line
pass through the middle of the data rather than being forced through the origin.
The Two Techniques
From the notes
Two techniques find the optimal $m$ and $c$:

head: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
Gradient Descent
rows: Use when columns / dimensions are low

blocks.t: Ordinary Least Squares
From the notes

The goal is to reduce the error — the distance of each point from the
line.
\boxed{ E(m,c)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i-mx_i-c\right)^{2} }
Find the optimal $m$ and $c$ for the lowest $E$.
Why squared, and not absolute

head: Reason
Squared $\sum d_i^2$
Absolute $\sum|d_i|$
rows: No — the modulus removes it too
MLE under Laplace noise; estimates the median

blocks.t: The decisive reason

Differentiability. The whole derivation below rests on setting
$\partial E/\partial m=0$ and $\partial E/\partial c=0$, and you cannot
differentiate $|d|$ at $d=0$. Squaring buys the closed form. The price is
sensitivity to outliers (Topic 28).
The derivation

blocks.cap:
$E(m,c)$ is a convex paraboloid in the two parameters. It has exactly
 one stationary point, and that point is the global minimum — which is why
 setting the derivatives to zero solves the problem completely.

blocks.t: Solve for $c$ first

\frac{\partial E}{\partial c}
 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2\left(y_i-mx_i-c\right)(-1) = 0

A useful fact falls out immediately: the best-fit line always passes through the
point $(\bar x,\bar y)$, the centroid of the data.
Then solve for $m$

\frac{\partial E}{\partial m}
 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2\left(y_i-mx_i-c\right)(-x_i)=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \sum_i x_i y_i - m\sum_i x_i^2 - c\sum_i x_i = 0 .
Substitute $c=\bar y-m\bar x$:
\sum_i x_iy_i - m\sum_i x_i^2 - (\bar y-m\bar x) n\bar x = 0 .
Collect the $m$ terms:
m\left(\sum_i x_i^2 - n\bar x^{2}\right) = \sum_i x_iy_i - n\bar x\bar y

using the identities $\sum x_iy_i-n\bar x\bar y=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)$
and $\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$.
Read the formula

The slope is covariance over variance. It answers: when $x$ moves
one unit away from its mean, how far does $y$ move? Two consequences worth
remembering:

items:
$m$ and the Pearson correlation are related by
 $m = r\,\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}$. The slope is the correlation, rescaled into
 the units of $y$ per unit of $x$.

If $\operatorname{Var}(x)=0$ — a constant column — the slope is
 undefined. There is no line to fit.

blocks.t: The matrix form
Generalising to any number of features

Write $X$ as an $n\times(p+1)$ matrix whose first column is all ones (absorbing
the intercept), and $\beta$ as the $(p+1)$-vector of coefficients. Then
E(\beta)=\|y-X\beta\|^2=(y-X\beta)^{ \top}(y-X\beta).
Differentiating with respect to $\beta$:

\frac{\partial E}{\partial\beta}=-2X^{ \top}(y-X\beta)=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 X^{ \top}X\beta = X^{ \top}y
— the normal equations, whose solution is
\boxed{ \hat\beta=\left(X^{ \top}X\right)^{-1}X^{ \top}y }

This is the same result: with one feature it reduces exactly to the $m$ and $c$
above. It is also the reason multicollinearity matters — if two columns are
perfectly correlated, $X^{\!\top}X$ is singular and the inverse does not exist
(Topics 15, 41).
The geometric view

$X\beta$ ranges over the column space of $X$ — a $(p+1)$-dimensional subspace of
$\mathbb{R}^n$. Minimising $\|y-X\beta\|$ means finding the point in that
subspace closest to $y$, which is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto
it. The normal equations state exactly that: the residual $y-X\hat\beta$ is
perpendicular to every column of $X$.

Two corollaries you can use as sanity checks: the residuals sum to zero (when an
intercept is fitted), and the residuals are uncorrelated with every predictor.
The Assumptions

OLS gives a number for any data. These assumptions decide whether that number
means anything.

head: Assumption
Statement
Check / consequence
rows: $\mathbb{E}[y\mid x]$ is linear in the parameters
Residual plot shows no curve; otherwise use polynomial regression
Residual plot shows no funnel; otherwise standard errors are wrong
Q-Q plot. Needed for inference, not for the point estimate

blocks.t: Gauss–Markov

Under linearity, exogeneity, homoscedasticity and uncorrelated errors, OLS is
BLUE — the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator: among all unbiased
estimators that are linear in $y$, it has the smallest variance. Note what is
not required: normality. That assumption is needed only for $t$-tests,
$p$-values and confidence intervals.
When to Use OLS, and When Not

blocks.cap:
The notes' rule, measured. OLS inverts a $p\times p$ matrix at
 $O(p^3)$ cost, so it is unbeatable for a handful of features and becomes
 impractical for thousands. Gradient descent scales linearly in $p$.

head: Use OLS when
Use gradient descent when
rows: Many features, or $p$ larger than memory allows
The data arrives as a stream (Topic 03)
You want the exact answer, once
You need an incremental / online fit
The loss has no closed form (logistic, neural nets)

blocks.t: Never literally invert the matrix

$(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ is the formula, not the algorithm. Forming
$X^{\!\top}X$ squares the condition number, and explicit inversion is both slower
and less stable than solving the linear system. Libraries use a QR decomposition
or the SVD — numpy.linalg.lstsq and scikit-learn's
LinearRegression both use SVD-based least squares, which also returns a
sensible answer when $X$ is rank-deficient.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200
cgpa = rng.uniform(5, 10, n)
pkg  = 1.9 * cgpa - 5.5 + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n)      # true m=1.9, c=-5.5

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE CLOSED FORM, DERIVED BY HAND
# =====================================================================
x_bar, y_bar = cgpa.mean(), pkg.mean()

num = np.sum((cgpa - x_bar) * (pkg - y_bar))         # covariance numerator
den = np.sum((cgpa - x_bar) ** 2)                    # variance numerator
m = num / den
c = y_bar - m * x_bar                                 # c = y_bar - m*x_bar

print(f"m = {m:.6f}   c = {c:.6f}")
print("matches sklearn:",
      np.allclose([m, c], [LinearRegression().fit(cgpa.reshape(-1,1), pkg).coef_[0],
                           LinearRegression().fit(cgpa.reshape(-1,1), pkg).intercept_]))

# The slope IS covariance over variance:
print(f"cov/var = {np.cov(cgpa, pkg, bias=True)[0,1] / np.var(cgpa):.6f}")

# And it is the correlation rescaled into the units of y per unit of x:
r = np.corrcoef(cgpa, pkg)[0, 1]
print(f"r * (sy/sx) = {r * pkg.std() / cgpa.std():.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE LINE PASSES THROUGH THE CENTROID -- a consequence of dE/dc = 0
# =====================================================================
print(f"\npredicted at x_bar: {m*x_bar + c:.6f}   y_bar: {y_bar:.6f}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. AS A CLASS
# =====================================================================
class SimpleLinearRegression:
    def fit(self, x, y):
        x, y = np.asarray(x).ravel(), np.asarray(y).ravel()
        xb, yb = x.mean(), y.mean()
        self.m_ = np.sum((x - xb) * (y - yb)) / np.sum((x - xb) ** 2)
        self.c_ = yb - self.m_ * xb
        return self

    def predict(self, x):
        return self.m_ * np.asarray(x).ravel() + self.c_

mine = SimpleLinearRegression().fit(cgpa, pkg)
print(f"\nscratch  m {mine.m_:.6f}  c {mine.c_:.6f}")
print(f"R2 {r2_score(pkg, mine.predict(cgpa)):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. WHY SQUARED AND NOT ABSOLUTE -- differentiability
# =====================================================================
grid = np.linspace(m - 1.5, m + 1.5, 601)
sq  = [np.sum((pkg - (mm*cgpa + c))**2) for mm in grid]
ab  = [np.sum(np.abs(pkg - (mm*cgpa + c))) for mm in grid]

d_sq = np.gradient(sq, grid); d_ab = np.gradient(ab, grid)
print(f"\nsquared loss: smooth, 2nd derivative constant "
      f"({np.std(np.gradient(d_sq, grid)):.2e} variation)")
print(f"absolute loss: kinked, gradient jumps by "
      f"{np.max(np.abs(np.diff(d_ab))):.2f} at the minimum")
# Only the smooth one lets you set dE/dm = 0 and solve.

# But absolute loss is ROBUST -- add three bad points and compare:
cg2 = np.r_[cgpa, [5.2, 5.4, 5.1]]
pk2 = np.r_[pkg,  [40.,  42.,  38.]]
print(f"\nOLS slope with 3 outliers: "
      f"{np.polyfit(cg2, pk2, 1)[0]:.3f}   (true 1.9)")
from sklearn.linear_model import HuberRegressor
print(f"Huber slope with 3 outliers: "
      f"{HuberRegressor().fit(cg2.reshape(-1,1), pk2).coef_[0]:.3f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE MATRIX FORM -- the same answer, and how to compute it properly
# =====================================================================
X = np.c_[np.ones(n), cgpa]                          # add the intercept column

beta_bad  = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ pkg       # the FORMULA
beta_ok   = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ pkg)      # solve, do not invert
beta_best = np.linalg.lstsq(X, pkg, rcond=None)[0]   # SVD -- what sklearn uses

print("\ninverse :", beta_bad.round(6))
print("solve   :", beta_ok.round(6))
print("lstsq   :", beta_best.round(6))
print(f"cond(X)     {np.linalg.cond(X):.2e}")
print(f"cond(X'X)   {np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X):.2e}   <- SQUARED, precision lost")

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE GEOMETRY -- residuals are orthogonal to the columns of X
# =====================================================================
resid = pkg - X @ beta_best
print(f"\nsum of residuals        {resid.sum():.2e}   (0 because c is fitted)")
print(f"resid . x               {(resid @ cgpa):.2e}   (orthogonal projection)")
print(f"corr(resid, fitted)     {np.corrcoef(resid, X @ beta_best)[0,1]:.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. CHECKING THE ASSUMPTIONS
# =====================================================================
from scipy import stats
fitted = X @ beta_best

# linearity + homoscedasticity: look for structure in the residual plot
sl, _, rr, pv, _ = stats.linregress(fitted, np.abs(resid))
print(f"\n|resid| vs fitted slope {sl:+.4f} (p={pv:.3f}) "
      f"{'-> heteroscedastic' if pv < .05 else '-> constant variance, OK'}")

# normality of errors -- needed for p-values, not for the point estimate
print(f"residual normality p = {stats.normaltest(resid)[1]:.3f}")

# standard errors, from the same matrix
sigma2 = (resid @ resid) / (n - X.shape[1])
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)))
t = beta_best / se
print(f"\n{'coef':>10s} {'std err':>10s} {'t':>8s} {'p':>10s}")
for name, b_, s_, t_ in zip(["intercept", "cgpa"], beta_best, se, t):
    p_ = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_), n - X.shape[1]))
    print(f"{name:>10s} {b_:10.4f} {s_:10.4f} {t_:8.2f} {p_:10.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. OLS vs GRADIENT DESCENT -- the notes' rule, measured
# =====================================================================
import time
print(f"\n{'p':>6s} {'OLS':>10s} {'SGD':>10s}")
for p in [1, 10, 100, 1000, 3000]:
    Xd = rng.normal(0, 1, (4000, p))
    yd = Xd @ rng.normal(0, 1, p) + rng.normal(0, .5, 4000)
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); LinearRegression().fit(Xd, yd); a = time.perf_counter()-t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); SGDRegressor(max_iter=60, tol=None).fit(Xd, yd)
    b = time.perf_counter()-t0
    print(f"{p:6d} {a:9.4f}s {b:9.4f}s")
# OLS is O(p^3): unbeatable when p is small, impractical when p is large.
Worked Examples
OLS by hand on five points
Step 1 – means. $\bar x = 3$, $\bar y = 4$.
Step 2 – slope.
Step 3 – intercept. $c = \bar y - m\bar x = 4 - 1.8 = 2.2$, so $\hat y = 0.6x + 2.2$.
Step 4 – predictions and residuals.
Step 5 – check. SSE $= 2.4$. Total sum of squares $= \sum (y-\bar y)^2 = 6$, so $R^2 = 1 - 2.4/6 = 0.60$. Also SSE $=$ $S_{yy} - m\,S_{xy} = 6 - 0.6\cdot 6 = 2.4$, which confirms the algebra.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Linear regression is supervised. Types: simple
 (1 input), multiple ($>1$ input), polynomial
 (non-linear data).

Simple linear regression finds the best-fit line with the lowest
 possible error from each point: $y=mx+c$, where $m$ is the slope and
 $c$ the $y$-intercept (the offset).

The goal is to find optimal $m$ and $c$, by OLS (use
 when dimensions are low) or gradient descent (use when
 dimensions are high).

Squared error is used because it is differentiable everywhere,
 which is what yields a closed form. Absolute error is more robust but has
 no closed form.

Setting $\partial E/\partial c=0$ gives $c=\bar y-m\bar x$ — so the line
 passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$.

Setting $\partial E/\partial m=0$ gives
 $m=\dfrac{\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2} =\dfrac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)} = r\,\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}$.

In matrix form $\hat\beta=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}y$ — the normal
 equations — which is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto the column
 space of $X$.

Assumptions: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of
 errors (for inference only), no perfect multicollinearity, exogeneity.
 Under Gauss–Markov, OLS is BLUE.
Never literally invert $X^{\!\top}X$ — use lstsq / SVD.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Derive the slope of a simple linear regression.

Write $E=\sum(y_i-mx_i-c)^2$. Set $\partial E/\partial c=0$ to get
$c=\bar y-m\bar x$. Substitute into $\partial E/\partial m=0$ and collect terms
to get $m=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)/\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$ — covariance over
variance.
Q. Why squared error rather than absolute error?

Differentiability. The closed-form solution comes from setting derivatives to
zero, and $|d|$ is not differentiable at zero. Squared error also has a clean
statistical interpretation — it is the maximum-likelihood estimator under
Gaussian noise — at the cost of sensitivity to outliers.
Q. When would you use gradient descent instead of the closed form?

When the number of features is large (the closed form is $O(p^3)$), when the data
does not fit in memory or arrives as a stream, or when the loss has no closed
form at all — logistic regression and neural networks.

Q. What does it mean that the residuals are orthogonal to the
predictors?

That $X\hat\beta$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto the column space of
$X$ — the closest point in the space of achievable predictions. Practically: the
residuals sum to zero when an intercept is fitted, and they are uncorrelated with
every predictor. Any pattern in a residual plot means the model has missed
structure.
Q. What is Gauss–Markov, and does it require normality?

It states that under linearity, exogeneity, homoscedasticity and uncorrelated
errors, OLS is the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator — minimum variance among
unbiased linear estimators. It does not require normality; that is needed
only for $t$-tests, $p$-values and confidence intervals.
Q. Your residual plot shows a funnel shape. What does that mean?

Heteroscedasticity — the error variance grows with the fitted value. The
coefficients remain unbiased, but the standard errors are wrong, so all inference
is invalid. Fix by transforming the target (log), using weighted least squares, or
using robust standard errors.
